converter.calibration: AC round-trip efficiency, auxiliary-excluded, from the year-one fitted curve of a 500 kW / 822 kWh NMC plant in southern Italy measured at 11 setpoints (doi:10.1016/j.est.2023.107232, Eq. 8 and Table 6): 0.937 round trip near rated, 0.771 at 0.1 p.u., entered as one-way 0.968 / 0.878 under the paper's symmetric convention
converter.calibration_note: that paper's better-known 0.85 / 0.65 pair is its *global* efficiency (Eq. 11), whose denominator includes auxiliary energy; calibrating to it while charging auxiliaries separately double-counts them, and most of its low-load droop is cycle duration (26.4 h per cycle at 0.1 p.u. against 2.6 h at rated) rather than part-load electronics

finding: the two errors inside a conventional flat-efficiency assumption have opposite signs, and for a 2-hour battery they nearly cancel unless a standing auxiliary load is present. With no thermal load the conventional model is 0.4 % low: a flat 0.9 round trip understates the real converter in the 86 %-of-rated band this asset actually discharges at, and that gain (+115,863 GBP) slightly exceeds the cost of the no-load draw it ignores (+107,972 GBP). Every pound of net overstatement therefore traces to the standing auxiliary load, rising roughly linearly with it to 16 % at 0.20 MW. Putting the curve inside the optimiser is worth 4.2-4.8 % and does move dispatch, pushing mean discharge load from 86.2% to 90.2% of rated, because an auxiliary-excluded curve rises monotonically toward rated power instead of peaking mid-load. The expensive omission is the auxiliary load; the flat efficiency itself is close to harmless here, and in the wrong direction from the usual assumption
